records.sourceFile: How do training and competition workloads related to      injury - The workload-injury aetiology model.pdf

paper.citation: Windt J, Gabbett TJ. How do training and competition workloads relate to injury? The workload-injury aetiology model. Br J Sports Med. 2016.
paper.abstract: The authors review injury aetiology models and workload-injury studies, then propose an updated model in which training and competition loads influence injury risk through exposure, fitness and fatigue. Total workload and acute:chronic workload spikes are linked to injury in the cited studies. The model is presented as a conceptual framework for future research.
paper.tldr: Workloads should be treated as the vehicle through which athletes are exposed to injury risk, and as a driver of both fitness and fatigue. Monitoring workload changes, not only total load, is likely to matter for injury risk.
paper.methods: Narrative review and conceptual model. No systematic search method is described. The authors discuss previous injury aetiology models and workload-injury studies, then propose the workload-injury aetiology model.
paper.findings: Previous aetiology models did not include training and competition workloads. The authors propose that workloads affect injury risk through exposure, fitness and fatigue. The review reports that acute:chronic workload spikes are strongly associated with injury in several sports, but the mechanisms remain unclear.
paper.limitations: The model is conceptual and has not been tested in a prospective study. The review does not describe how studies were identified, so the evidence it draws on cannot be checked for completeness. The authors acknowledge that many risk-factor interactions are unknown.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use the model to frame workload monitoring as part of injury prevention, tracking both total load and how quickly it changes. The cited evidence favours building high chronic loads while keeping week-to-week changes within about 10% and avoiding acute:chronic spikes, though these figures come from a small number of team-sport cohorts.
paper.athleteDev: Build training loads gradually and keep acute increases from outpacing chronic preparation, so that fitness gains are not offset by fatigue and injury risk. Track workload over time as well as total volume.
paper.rtp: The review cites data from cricket, rugby league and Australian football linking acute:chronic workload ratios to injury risk during return to play, so it can frame how load is rebuilt after injury. It does not provide validated return-to-play thresholds and should not be used alone to clear an athlete for full training.

records.sourceFile: How much is too much - IOC consensus statement on load       in sport and risk of illness Part 2.pdf

paper.citation: Schwellnus M, Soligard T, Alonso JM, Bahr R, Clarsen B, Dijkstra HP, et al. How much is too much? (Part 2) International Olympic Committee consensus statement on load in sport and risk of illness. Br J Sports Med. 2016;50:1043-1052.
paper.abstract: An IOC expert group reviewed evidence on how training, competition, psychological and travel load relate to acute illness and overtraining in athletes. The statement summarises the load-illness evidence and sets out practical guidelines for load management, illness monitoring and illness prevention. It also identifies urgent research priorities.
paper.tldr: Very high training loads can raise illness risk in recreational and subelite athletes, and the pattern may differ in top elite athletes. Staff should monitor external and internal load, change loads gradually, manage psychological stress and plan recovery, while recognising that illness risk cannot yet be quantified.
paper.methods: Consensus statement by an IOC expert group that met in November 2015. Members reviewed the literature independently, and a post hoc search of four databases (1980 to March 2016) identified 796 unique studies after duplicates were removed. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts, 30 publications were included in the load-illness analysis, and recommendations were agreed by consensus.
paper.findings: Absolute training load showed a J-shaped relationship with illness in recreational and subelite athletes, while high-level elite athletes may show a different pattern with lower illness risk at high loads. Increases in training volume were associated with more illness in several studies, and competition was an independent risk factor for illness (odds ratio 2.9) in one cohort of elite cross-country skiers. In one study of elite rugby union players, travel across more than four time zones was associated with two to three times the risk of illness. The authors state that the data are not yet sufficient to quantify illness risk for a given load or load change.
paper.limitations: This is an expert consensus document, so recommendations reflect judgement applied to heterogeneous studies that are mostly observational. Most illness data were self-reported, all studies measured external load but only some measured internal load or load changes, and few used multiple risk factor modelling, as the authors acknowledge. The weekly increase limit of under 10% is drawn from the injury literature rather than from illness data.
paper.practicalImplications: Medical staff can build an illness-prevention plan covering hygiene, sleep, nutrition, vaccination and early symptom monitoring, and track both external and internal load. Training loads should change in small weekly steps, with planned recovery after intense blocks, competitions and travel. Because quantitative thresholds are not established, these measures are a framework for judgement rather than fixed limits.
paper.athleteDev: Plan training and competition loads in gradual steps, and build in recovery after congested competition blocks and long-haul travel. Track how athletes respond as well as the volume they complete, because the same external load can produce different internal responses.
paper.rtp: The statement addresses illness prevention and load management, not return to sport after injury, and it gives no return-to-sport criteria. Its principle of gradual load increase could inform a return to training, but the paper sets no thresholds for that use.

records.sourceFile: How much is too much - IOC consensus statement on load      in sport and risk of injury Part 1.pdf

paper.citation: Soligard T, Schwellnus M, Alonso JM, Bahr R, Clarsen B, Dijkstra HP, et al. How much is too much? (Part 1) International Olympic Committee consensus statement on load in sport and risk of injury. Br J Sports Med. 2016;50:1030-1041.
paper.abstract: The International Olympic Committee convened an expert group to review evidence linking load (training and competition load, calendar congestion, psychological load and travel) to health outcomes in sport. The consensus summarises the links between load and injury, gives practical guidelines for prescribing and monitoring load, and identifies research priorities.
paper.tldr: Rapid increases in load, relative to what an athlete is prepared for, are a major injury risk factor. Load should be prescribed and monitored individually, using a combination of external and internal measures, because no single marker has been validated.
paper.methods: Expert consensus meeting, followed by a post hoc literature search of PubMed (including MEDLINE) and SPORTDiscus limited to English-language studies published before June 2016. The consensus group included 104 publications in the review and agreed the final guidelines by consensus.
paper.findings: Studies on absolute load gave mixed results: high load was linked to injury in several sports but was not, or was protective, in others. Studies in several team sports associated large week-to-week load increases with higher injury risk. In data from Australian football, cricket and rugby league, injury likelihood was below 10% with an acute:chronic load ratio of 0.8 to 1.3 and more than doubled when the ratio exceeded 1.5. In football, two matches per week compared with one was associated with higher match injury risk, and no link to injury was established for travel.
paper.limitations: The authors note heterogeneity in sports, samples, load and injury definitions, and designs. Many congestion studies used small single-team samples, ignored player rotation, or used retrospective cross-sectional designs, and the acute:chronic ratio was validated in only three sports. No single marker has been validated to identify maladaptation.
paper.practicalImplications: Avoid rapid increases in load. Based on evidence from Australian football, cricket and rugby league, the statement suggests limiting weekly increases to under 10% or keeping the acute:chronic load ratio within 0.8 to 1.3. In football, consider squad rotation when two matches fall in one week, and monitor load with a combination of external and internal measures, including subjective well-being scales.
paper.athleteDev: Keep week-to-week load increases modest and use an acute:chronic load ratio of 0.8 to 1.3 as a monitoring reference rather than a hard threshold. Prescribe and adjust load individually, combining external load data with subjective measures, because no single marker has been validated. In football, consider squad rotation when two matches fall in one week.
paper.rtp: The statement does not address return to sport or rehabilitation criteria. Its load ranges come from injury studies in healthy athletes, so they should not be used to set return-to-play loads for an injured athlete.

records.sourceFile: ISCHRO~1.PDF

paper.citation: Luan L, Witchalls J, Ganderton C, Adams R, El-Ansary D, Han J. Is chronic ankle instability associated with contractile thickness of gluteus medius and gluteus maximus during functional movement and exercise? A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2024;64.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of ultrasound-measured contractile thickness of the gluteus medius and gluteus maximus during functional movement and exercise in people with chronic ankle instability (CAI). Six observational studies with 176 participants were identified, and four were pooled. The authors report lower gluteus medius activity in CAI, no significant difference in gluteus maximus, and a weaker correlation between the two muscles in CAI than in controls.
paper.tldr: People with chronic ankle instability may recruit the gluteus medius less during functional movement than people without it, while gluteus maximus activity looks similar. Few studies, high heterogeneity and graph-derived values mean this should be treated as a trend.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, searching six databases to 15 January 2024 for observational studies of ultrasound-measured gluteal thickness in CAI versus controls during physical activity. Included studies were scored with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and graded with GRADE. Outcomes were functional activity ratios (thickness during activity divided by thickness at rest), pooled in RevMan, and GMed and GMax correlations and differences were analysed in CAI and control groups.
paper.findings: Across four pooled studies, gluteus medius FAR was lower in CAI than in controls (WMD -0.08, 95% CI -0.11 to -0.04; P < 0.00001; I2 74%), and it was also lower in both the walking and the elementary movement or resistance-exercise subgroups (I2 0% in each). Gluteus maximus FAR did not differ (WMD 0.02, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.05; P = 0.25; I2 71%). In the CAI group, GMed and GMax FAR were only weakly correlated (PCC 0.397) and differed from each other (t-test P = 0.029), whereas in controls the correlation was moderate (PCC 0.627) with no difference (P = 0.354).
paper.limitations: Only four studies were pooled, the samples were small, and the included participants differed in sex, height, weight, age and control-limb choice. Some FAR values were digitized from graphs, which the authors say may reduce precision. The GRADE table lists '15 (528)' trials and participants for each overview, which appears to count task-level comparisons rather than the 6 studies and 176 participants reported in the abstract and text.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians could assess gluteus medius recruitment during functional tasks in people with CAI, and the authors suggest prioritizing gluteus medius strengthening. The studies do not show that gluteus medius training corrects recruitment deficits or reduces instability, so any program should be judged on patient outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not measure performance. Its one practical suggestion is to consider gluteus medius recruitment and strengthening in people with CAI, since pelvic and single-leg control matter in sport; gluteus maximus activity looked similar to controls.
paper.rtp: The review addresses people with chronic ankle instability, a common outcome of ankle sprain, but it does not study return to sport or re-injury. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or to show that gluteal retraining reduces re-injury.

records.sourceFile: Imaging-detected sports injuries and imaging-guided interventions in athletes during the 2022 FIFA soccer World Cup.pdf

paper.citation: Bordalo M, Serner A, Yamashiro E, Al-Musa E, Djadoun MA, Al-Khelaifi K, et al. Imaging-detected sports injuries and imaging-guided interventions in athletes during the 2022 FIFA football (soccer) World Cup. Skeletal Radiology. 2023.
paper.abstract: Retrospective analysis of all radiology examinations at the central medical facility for players during the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar. Of 143 examinations in 94 athletes, MRI accounted for 67%, and 112 injuries were recorded, mostly muscle and tendon (42%), ligament (25%) and cartilage (21%) injuries. Image-guided interventions were 8% of examinations, and imaging was used for 11% of players.
paper.tldr: At the 2022 World Cup, about 11% of players needed imaging at the central facility, mostly MRI. Muscle and tendon injuries, mainly acute grade 1 and 2 tears in the thigh, were the most common imaging findings.
paper.methods: Retrospective cohort of all radiology examinations for players who attended the Aspetar central medical facility from 10 November to 19 December 2022. Two musculoskeletal radiologists independently reviewed MRI, ultrasound, radiography and CT, with a third reader resolving disagreements, and classified injuries using IOC tissue categories and imaging grading systems. Image-guided procedures were recorded from the same images and reports.
paper.findings: Of 143 examinations for 94 players, 112 injuries were found, most often in the thigh (27%), ankle and foot (23%) and knee (23%). Muscle and tendon injuries were 42% of injuries, and 95% of muscle injuries were acute, with grade 1 and grade 2 tears making up most cases. Eleven players had imaging-guided injections, and eight of them (72%) returned to play during the tournament.
paper.limitations: Clinical information was limited and there was no clinical or surgical correlation, and return-to-play data were incomplete. The authors also had no access to ultrasound performed by team medical staff or to imaging done outside the facility.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff planning imaging for a major tournament should expect MRI to be the main modality, with muscle injuries and ankle ligament and cartilage findings common. The central-facility model gave one overview of imaging use, but the authors do not show that it improved outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: Imaging at this tournament was mostly MRI for thigh, groin and knee problems, and the common findings were muscle tears, ankle ligament tears and cartilage lesions. The study does not show whether these injuries or imaging choices affected performance.
paper.rtp: The study reports that 8 of 11 players who received imaging-guided injections returned to play during the tournament, but it has no return-to-play timelines or outcomes. It cannot be used to set return-to-play timing or to show whether injections or MRI findings predict return.

records.sourceFile: Immediate Removal From Activity After Sport-Related Concussion Is Associated With Shorter Clinical Recovery and Less Severe Symptoms in Collegiate Student-Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Asken BM, Bauer RM, Guskiewicz KM, McCrea MA, Schmidt JD, Giza CC, et al. Immediate Removal From Activity After Sport-Related Concussion Is Associated With Shorter Clinical Recovery and Less Severe Symptoms in Collegiate Student-Athletes. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;46(6):1465-1474.
paper.abstract: Cohort analysis of CARE Consortium data on 506 concussions in collegiate and military-academy athletes across 18 sports. Athletes removed from activity immediately (n = 184) lost about 3 fewer days from sport than delayed-removal athletes (n = 322), had shorter symptom duration, and had lower risk of needing 14 or 21 days to full clearance. They also had fewer and less severe acute symptoms, and the authors describe immediate removal as a protective factor.
paper.tldr: Athletes removed from play immediately after a concussion recovered faster and had milder early symptoms than those who kept playing. The design is observational, so the result may partly reflect injury severity and reporting patterns.
paper.methods: Cohort analysis of the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium concussion database. Athletes were classified as immediate or delayed removal from activity using two clinician questions. Outcomes were time lost from sport, symptom duration, and acute clinical scores (SCAT3, BSI-18, SAC, BESS), analysed with three-step hierarchical regression, 20 multiple imputations, and multivariate and univariate tests.
paper.findings: Immediate removal was the only factor that significantly predicted time lost, with about 3 fewer days lost (pooled B = 2.95) and about 2 days shorter symptom duration (pooled B = 2.02). Immediate removal was also linked to lower risk of needing 14 days (RR 0.614) or 21 days (RR 0.534) to full clearance, and to fewer and less severe SCAT3 symptoms at 0 to 6 hours and 24 to 48 hours and lower BSI-18 scores at 24 to 48 hours. SAC and BESS scores did not differ, and loss or alteration of consciousness was more common in the immediate-removal group.
paper.limitations: The main limit is missing data: only 506 of 815 concussions had complete data, and the authors assume the included cases represent the full set. Removal timing and symptom report relied on clinician and athlete recall, and some athletes with delayed symptom onset may have been classified inconsistently. The abstract lists 25 institutions, while the Methods list 22.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes, coaches and clinicians should be taught to report concussion symptoms and stop activity immediately, since the study links immediate removal with shorter recovery. The paper supports education about symptom reporting rather than a specific removal protocol, and it cannot show that stopping play sooner causes faster recovery.
paper.athleteDev: The study is about concussion recovery rather than performance. For performance and athletic staff, the message is to make immediate reporting and removal from practice or games routine, because delayed removal was linked to longer time out of sport.
paper.rtp: The study bears directly on return to sport, since immediate removal was associated with shorter time to full clearance. It does not set clearance criteria, and its outcome is time to clearance rather than the safety of return, so it should not be used alone to decide return to play.

records.sourceFile: In it to Win it - Competitiveness Concussion Knowledge and Nondisclosure in Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Doucette MM, du Plessis S, Webber AM, Whalen C, Garcia-Barrera MA. In it to Win it: Competitiveness, Concussion Knowledge and Nondisclosure in Athletes. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional survey of 161 Canadian athletes aged 14 to 32 years examined concussion knowledge, attitudes and competitiveness in relation to past concussion nondisclosure and intention to keep playing with symptoms. Competitiveness was associated with both outcomes, and concussion knowledge was not.
paper.tldr: Among 161 young athletes, more competitive athletes were more likely to report having kept playing after a suspected concussion and more likely to say they would keep playing with symptoms. Concussion knowledge did not explain either outcome.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional paper survey completed anonymously and under supervision by athletes from teams recruited through coaches. The survey included a modified Rosenbaum Concussion Attitude and Knowledge Survey, the 25-item Sport Orientation Questionnaire for competitiveness, a yes/no item on past nondisclosure and a 5-point item on continuing to play with a headache from a minor concussion. Binomial (past nondisclosure) and ordinal (intention) logistic regressions included competitiveness, knowledge, age, sex and sport.
paper.findings: Of the 161 athletes, 44% reported having received what they thought was a concussion and kept playing without telling anyone. Higher competitiveness was associated with past nondisclosure (OR 1.03 per point, p = .03) and with intention to play with symptoms (OR 1.05 per point, p < .01), and rowers were less likely than collision-sport athletes to report past nondisclosure (OR 0.13). Concussion knowledge, age and sex were not significant in either model. Soccer players and females scored higher on knowledge, but the authors describe these differences as small and possibly not clinically meaningful.
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional, the sample was male-majority (71%), only one non-collision contact sport and one noncontact sport were recruited, recruitment was through coaches, and each model explains about 18% of variance. The Results text gives the 97.5% CI for the intention model as 1.003 to 1.06, but Table 3 and the abstract give 1.03 to 1.08 (1.003 to 1.06 is the past-nondisclosure CI). Some Table 3 standard errors look like typing errors (age 2.20 and sex .05 in the past-nondisclosure model). The intention outcome is a single Likert item, and the file is the accepted author manuscript.
paper.practicalImplications: Programs that aim to improve concussion reporting could be designed to reach highly competitive athletes, as the authors suggest, rather than relying on knowledge campaigns alone. The study does not show that this targeting reduces nondisclosure, and it can only support asking about competitive drive as a risk marker in a conversation.
paper.athleteDev: The study is about concussion reporting, not performance outcomes. Its relevance for performance staff is limited to how the athlete's competitive drive may affect honest symptom reporting during training and competition.
paper.rtp: The study does not measure recovery, return-to-play decisions or post-concussion symptom management. It may help flag athletes at higher risk of hiding symptoms, but it cannot set return-to-play criteria or clearance steps.

records.sourceFile: Incidence and prevalence of hamstring injuries in field-based team sports - A systematic review and meta-analysis of 5952 injuries from over 7 m.pdf

paper.citation: Maniar N, Carmichael DS, Hickey JT, Timmins RG, San Jose AJ, Dickson J, Opar D. Incidence and prevalence of hamstring injuries in field-based team sports: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 5952 injuries from over 7 million exposure hours. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 63 prospective cohort studies in six field-based team sports pooled 5952 hamstring injuries over about 7.26 million exposure hours. The pooled hamstring injury incidence was 0.81 per 1000 hours, and the 9-month prevalence was 13%. Incidence was higher in matches than in training and on grass than on artificial turf, and it rose with average cohort age.
paper.tldr: Hamstring injuries made up about 10 percent of all injuries in these team sports, with about 13 percent of athletes injured over a 9-month period. Matches carried a much higher injury rate than training, and the findings suggest the rate has not fallen over 30 years.
paper.methods: Systematic search of six databases from inception to August 2020, limited to prospective cohort studies of hamstring injury with total exposure hours in field-based team sports. Two authors screened titles and abstracts, three assessed full texts, and two rated quality with the JBI Critical Appraisal Tool for prevalence studies. Random-effects (multilevel) meta-analysis and meta-regression were used, with a protocol registered on PROSPERO.
paper.findings: Pooled hamstring injury incidence was 0.81 per 1000 hours (95% CI 0.66 to 0.98; prediction interval 0.18 to 3.70) and prevalence was 13% over 9 months (95% CI 9.5% to 17.6%). Match incidence was 3.85 vs 0.41 per 1000 hours in training (p < 0.001), and grass incidence was 0.72 vs 0.48 per 1000 hours on artificial turf in soccer (p < 0.001). Incidence rose 6.4% per year of average cohort age (p = 0.003), and sport, body mass, stature and year of data did not significantly moderate incidence. Hamstring strain injury alone had an incidence of 0.67 per 1000 hours.
paper.limitations: Heterogeneity was very high, and the included studies used different injury definitions (hamstring injury, hamstring strain injury and posterior thigh injury). Most data came from soccer and rugby union, many cohorts reported one pooled value for multiple seasons, previous injury could not be modelled, and women contributed only about 310,000 exposure hours. The abstract attaches p = 0.003 to the 9.4-fold match vs training difference, but the results give p < 0.001 for match vs training and p = 0.003 for age, and hamstring strain prevalence is 9.8% in the results but 9.7% in the discussion.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff in these sports can expect more hamstring injuries in matches than in training, and the authors suggest that training may not reproduce the high-intensity running demands of matches, so match-specific preparation deserves attention. The surface result is based on limited exposure hours, so it supports checking surfaces rather than treating artificial turf as a proven preventive measure.
paper.athleteDev: The study reports injury epidemiology, not performance outcomes. Its most useful point for performance staff is that match exposure carries a much higher hamstring injury rate than training, which should inform how match running demands are planned.
paper.rtp: The study does not evaluate rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions. It gives context on how often hamstring injuries occur, which can inform injury planning, but it cannot set return-to-play criteria or timelines.

records.sourceFile: Increased anterior pelvic tilt angle elevates the risk of hamstring injuries in soccer player.pdf

paper.citation: Bayrak A, Patlar S. Increased anterior pelvic tilt angle elevates the risk of hamstring injuries in soccer player. Research in Sports Medicine. 2024.
paper.abstract: This study examined whether anterior pelvic tilt (APT) angle is associated with hamstring injury in male professional football players followed over five years. Injured and non-injured players were compared with t-tests, regression and ROC analysis to find an APT cut-off. The authors report that higher APT was associated with more hamstring injuries, with a cut-off of 13 degrees.
paper.tldr: In 76 male professional footballers followed for five years, higher standing anterior pelvic tilt was associated with hamstring injury, and the authors derived a 13 degree cut-off. The cut-off comes from the same players and has not been validated, so it is a hypothesis for screening and not a clinical threshold.
paper.methods: Retrospective study of first-team players from one Premier Division club over five seasons. Standing APT (caliper inclinometer), knee posture, Q angle and tibial torsion were measured by one physiotherapist, and the authors state that APT was documented before injury; hamstring injuries causing at least three days out were confirmed by MRI. Analyses used independent t-tests, multiple linear regression and ROC analysis to set a cut-off.
paper.findings: Injured players (n = 33) had higher right and left APT than non-injured players (n = 43), about 14.1 and 14.2 degrees vs 9.7 degrees. The ROC cut-off was 13 degrees for both sides, with AUC 0.87 (right) and 0.88 (left), sensitivity of 69.7 to 72.7 percent and specificity of 93.0 percent. Q angle, tibial torsion and knee posture were not significant for overall hamstring injury.
paper.limitations: The Discussion states that 'a lower APT angle increases hamstring injuries' and gives a pooled mean APT of 14.54 degrees, both of which conflict with the Results tables (higher APT in injured players; injured about 14.1 to 14.2 degrees, non-injured about 9.7 degrees), so the table values are reported here. The Methods describe t-tests but Table 8 reports z values, Table 5 coefficients are garbled, and the 13 degree cut-off was derived and tested on the same players. The retrospective design, single male club sample and lack of exposure, strength or training-load data limit causal and general conclusions.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could record standing APT in pre-season screening as one possible risk marker, alongside other factors such as strength and flexibility. Because sensitivity was about 70 percent, a 13 degree threshold would miss many injured players, so it should not be used alone to decide who receives prevention work until it is validated in an independent group.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not measure performance. Its discussion cites other work suggesting that higher pelvic tilt can aid sprint speed while increasing hamstring strain, and this study does not test that trade-off.
paper.rtp: The study cannot show that adjusting pelvic tilt reduces hamstring injury, and it does not test any intervention or return-to-play outcome. It should not be used to set return-to-play criteria or to clear players for training or matches.

records.sourceFile: Individual Region- and   Muscle-specific Hamstring Activity at Different Running Speeds.pdf

paper.citation: Hegyi A, Gonçalves BAM, Finni T, Cronin NJ. Individual Region- and Muscle-specific Hamstring Activity at Different Running Speeds. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019.
paper.abstract: This laboratory study measured proximal-distal and muscle-specific activity of the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus during treadmill running at three speeds in 13 healthy amateur male athletes, using high-density surface EMG. EMG rose with running speed in all regions of both muscles, and each individual kept a similar activity pattern across speeds. The authors conclude that individual hamstring activity patterns are highly variable but consistent across speeds, which may support early submaximal running after hamstring injury.
paper.tldr: During treadmill running, hamstring EMG rose with speed and peaked in late swing, with large differences between individuals and little group-level difference between muscles or regions. The study tested healthy amateur men at submaximal speeds, so the authors' suggestion about early running after injury is a hypothesis, not a tested result.
paper.methods: Repeated-measures laboratory study of 13 male athletes from football and Gaelic football. Participants ran at 4.1, 5.4 and 6.8 m/s (about 45, 60 and 75 percent of maximum speed) while high-density surface EMG, kinematics and foot contact timing were recorded. EMG was normalised to maximal voluntary isometric contraction and analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA using statistical parametric mapping.
paper.findings: EMG activity increased with running speed in all regions of both muscles, peaking in late swing (BFlh about 63, 90 and 115 percent MVIC; ST about 69, 102 and 121 percent at the three speeds, as mean with 95 percent confidence limit). Group-level differences between proximal, middle and distal regions, and between BFlh and ST, were not significant at any speed. Individual activity patterns were highly variable between people but similar across speeds, and changes in muscle-tendon length in late swing were small.
paper.limitations: The sample was 13 healthy amateur men, the fastest speed was submaximal, and running was on a treadmill, so the results may not generalise to sprinting, overground running, women or injured athletes. Surface EMG is affected by cross-talk, and the authors note that the EMG normalisation could influence absolute values, although speed trends are unaffected. The authors also report that the cost and benefit of individual hamstring profiling is unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could expect hamstring EMG to rise steeply with running speed, with high late-swing activity at sprint-related speeds in healthy amateur athletes. The authors suggest that early submaximal running after hamstring injury may support neuromuscular recovery, but this was not tested in injured players and should be treated as a hypothesis for monitoring and trial designs.
paper.athleteDev: Hamstring EMG reached about 115 to 121 percent of MVIC in late swing at the fastest speed, and each athlete showed a consistent but individual activation pattern. Staff could consider individual hamstring activation profiles when choosing hamstring exercises, but the study does not test any training or performance outcome.
paper.rtp: The study tested healthy amateur men, so it cannot show that submaximal running after hamstring injury restores normal neuromuscular function or lowers reinjury risk. It should not be used alone to set running progressions or return-to-sport criteria.

records.sourceFile: Injectable Peptide Therapy - A Primer for Orthopaedic and Sports Medicine Physicians.pdf

paper.citation: Mayfield CK, Bolia IK, Feingold CL, Lin EH, Liu JN, Hatch GFR, et al. Injectable Peptide Therapy: A Primer for Orthopaedic and Sports Medicine Physicians. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2026;54(1):223-229.
paper.abstract: This narrative review examines the current evidence for six injectable peptides marketed for regenerative medicine and sports performance: BPC-157, TB-4, TB-500, CJC-1295 with ipamorelin, tesamorelin and GHK-Cu. It summarizes preclinical, case-level and clinical data for each peptide. The authors conclude that the evidence does not yet support clinical use and that dosing, frequency and duration are unknown.
paper.tldr: Injectable peptides such as BPC-157 and TB-500 are widely sold for injury recovery, but the review finds only animal data and one uncontrolled human knee series. Several of these peptides are on anti-doping lists, so athlete use raises doping and safety questions as well as clinical ones.
paper.methods: Narrative review of PubMed-indexed biochemical and clinical studies on six popular injectable peptides. The paper does not report search terms, date limits or screening steps, and it does not appraise study quality.
paper.findings: BPC-157 improved tendon, ligament, muscle and bone healing in animal models, but no randomized orthopedic trials exist. A 12-patient case series reported knee pain improvement in 11 patients after intra-articular BPC-157, with no control group and no quantitative outcome. TB-4 and TB-500 showed tissue repair in preclinical models, and no human orthopedic studies were found. CJC-1295 with ipamorelin and GHK-Cu have animal or non-orthopedic data only, and tesamorelin has no orthopedic studies. The authors state that BPC-157, TB-4/TB-500 and tesamorelin are on the WADA Prohibited List, and that FDA has placed several of these peptides in category 2 for compounding safety concerns.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative, with no reported search strategy or quality appraisal, and it relies on mostly animal and preclinical evidence. The only human orthopedic data is one uncontrolled case series with flawed methods, and the authors note that dosing, frequency and duration are unknown.
paper.practicalImplications: Check WADA and USADA status before discussing any injectable peptide with an athlete, and refer doping questions to the team physician and anti-doping staff. Explain that BPC-157 and TB-500 have no human orthopedic trial data, and that the single human BPC-157 series had no control group. Record the product source, since the review notes that peptides are sold as research chemicals and that compounding impurities are a concern.
paper.athleteDev: The review describes proposed muscle and performance effects for CJC-1295 with ipamorelin and GHK-Cu, but it finds no human data showing muscle growth or performance gains from these peptides. Staff should not recommend these peptides for performance use.
paper.rtp: The review gives no return-to-sport guidance. It cannot be used to decide whether an injured athlete can return to play or to support peptide use as a recovery aid, because the only human injury data is one uncontrolled knee injection series.

records.sourceFile: Injectable Testosterone Replacement Therapy Within 1 Year Before ACL Reconstruction Is Associated With Increased Revision Rates.pdf

paper.citation: Stickels MW, Brazier B, Parmar R, Cronen A, Hui C, Shah A. Injectable Testosterone Replacement Therapy Within 1 Year Before ACL Reconstruction Is Associated With Increased Revision Rates. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2026;14(1):23259671251399845.
paper.abstract: This retrospective cohort study compares anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) revision rates in patients who received injectable testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) before surgery with matched controls. TRT use within 1 year before the primary ACLR was associated with a higher revision rate, while TRT exposure at any time showed no difference. The authors suggest that counseling about this risk may be warranted in shared decision-making.
paper.tldr: Injectable testosterone in the year before ACL reconstruction was linked to a 3.3-fold higher revision rate (17.05% vs 5.17%) in a matched claims cohort. The study is retrospective, has no dose data and shows large baseline imbalances, so it supports counseling rather than a firm rule.
paper.methods: Retrospective PearlDiver claims cohort of patients with primary ACLR from 2015 to 2022 and at least 2 years of follow-up, using ICD-10 and CPT codes. Injectable TRT users were propensity-matched to non-users on age, sex and Charlson score, and revision was compared in three exposure intervals with univariate tests and log-rank analysis.
paper.findings: Injectable TRT within 1 year before ACLR was associated with revision in 66 of 387 patients (17.05%) vs 20 of 387 controls (5.17%), relative risk 3.30 (95% CI 2.04 to 5.33, P < .001). The Kaplan-Meier difference appeared at about 400 days. Distant use (more than 1 year before surgery) had 23 revisions among 160 patients (14.38%), but controls had too few revisions for a valid comparison. Any TRT exposure before or after surgery showed 6.36% vs 6.21% revision (P = .82).
paper.limitations: The study is retrospective and claims-based, with no dose, formulation detail, indication, graft type, surgical technique or activity level, and the authors note that people seeking TRT may be more physically active. Table 2 shows the groups still differed on hypogonadism (55.8% vs 3.4%), obesity, osteoarthritis and erectile dysfunction after matching. The distant-use and post-operative subgroups are underpowered, the Results text gives n = 2,614 for the any-exposure group while Tables 1 and 4 give 2,641, and the fold-change in the extracted conclusion is garbled ('.3-fold'), so rely on the reported relative risk of 3.30.
paper.practicalImplications: When counseling a patient who is on injectable testosterone and facing ACL reconstruction, present the reported association (17.05% vs 5.17% revision with exposure in the prior year) and its uncertainty. The authors suggest considering stopping TRT up to a year before elective ACLR, and delaying surgery where feasible, but the study did not test whether this changes outcomes. The any-exposure analysis found no difference, so do not extend the finding to post-operative use.
paper.athleteDev: The paper measures no performance outcome. Its relevance for athletes is a possible graft-outcome risk for those on injectable testosterone before ACL surgery, which should be raised with the team physician rather than used to guide training or performance decisions.
paper.rtp: The study bears on return to sport only indirectly, since revision is a major setback. It gives no return criteria or timelines, and the authors note that the revision code does not confirm graft failure.

records.sourceFile: Injury in starting and replacement players from five professional men's rugby unions.pdf

paper.citation: Roberts SP, Stokes KA, Williams S, West SW, Kemp S, Cross M, et al. Injury in Starting and Replacement Players from Five Professional Men's Rugby Unions. Sports Medicine. 2024.
paper.abstract: This study compares the incidence, severity and burden of time-loss injuries in starting and replacement players across professional men's teams in five rugby unions. It also tests whether one team's use of replacements is associated with injuries to the opposing team. The authors find no overall difference in incidence, a lower replacement incidence in the second half of matches, and a higher injury burden for replacements.
paper.tldr: Across five professional rugby unions over three seasons, starters and replacements had similar overall injury rates, but replacement injuries cost more days lost. Replacements were injured less often than starters in the last two match quarters, which suggests fatigue or interaction effects but does not prove them.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional analysis of time-loss match injuries and player minutes for starters (shirt numbers 1 to 15) and replacements (16 to 23) from English Premiership, Welsh Pro14 and Super Rugby teams, 2016 to 2019. Incidence, severity and burden were compared using rate ratios, and generalised linear mixed models tested whether one team's replacement use predicted injuries to the opponent.
paper.findings: Overall incidence was 78.2 per 1000 hours for starters and 77.0 for replacements (rate ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.10), and concussion incidence did not differ. Mean burden was higher for replacements (rate ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.46), with median injury severity 14.5 vs 12.0 days. Replacement incidence was lower in the third quarter (rate ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.92) and fourth quarter (0.78, 0.67 to 0.92), with the fourth-quarter difference driven by forwards. Burden met the authors' both-mean-and-median rule for lower-limb injuries (mean rate ratio 1.24, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.46) and for the tackled player (1.30, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.66), and head and neck injury severity was higher for replacements (median 11 vs 9 days). The number of replacements or replacement minutes a team used did not change the injury count or burden of the opposing team.
paper.limitations: The design is observational, and the study does not capture injury mechanism, activity intensity or replacement entry reason, such as blood or head injury assessment. Data collection tools varied between unions. The lower-limb median burden rate ratio is printed as 1.19 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.40), and it counts as significant only because the unrounded lower limit is 1.003, so the lower-limb burden result is borderline. The authors note limited ability to extrapolate to teams with fewer replacements.
paper.practicalImplications: Plan for replacement injuries to cost more time, since mean burden was about 31% higher, rather than assuming a replacement carries more injury risk over a full match. The second-half pattern (fewer replacement injuries) is an observational finding, so use it to inform discussion, not to change rotation rules. The authors' finding that opponents' replacement use did not change injury counts also argues against treating substitutions as a clear injury-risk lever.
paper.athleteDev: The study measures match injuries and minutes, not performance. The authors cite other studies reporting higher early running intensity in replacements, but they did not measure intensity here, so the link to performance and load is untested.
paper.rtp: The study bears on return to sport only indirectly, through the higher days lost for replacement injuries (median severity 14.5 vs 12.0 days). It gives no return criteria or protocols and cannot guide return-to-play decisions for individual players.

records.sourceFile: Injury reduction programs for reducing the incidence of sport-related head and neck injuries including concussion - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Elliott J, Heron N, Versteegh T, Gilchrist IA, Webb M, Archbold P, et al. Injury Reduction Programs for Reducing the Incidence of Sport-Related Head and Neck Injuries Including Concussion: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2021.
paper.abstract: This systematic review of six studies examined whether neck strength is linked to sport-related concussion (SRC) and whether neck exercise programs reduce head and neck injuries and SRC in athletes. Higher neck strength was associated with lower SRC risk in one observational study, and neck exercise programs were associated with lower injury rates in the intervention studies, with the strength of evidence varying by study.
paper.tldr: Six studies suggest that higher neck strength may be linked to lower concussion risk and that neck exercises within injury-prevention programs may reduce head and neck injuries. The authors describe this as limited evidence, and the clearest result comes from one adult rugby trial.
paper.methods: A PRISMA systematic review, registered on PROSPERO (194217), searched five databases to May 2020 for athlete studies that measured neck strength or included a neck exercise intervention. Methodological quality was rated with the Downs and Black checklist, and risk ratios and incidence rate ratios were calculated from raw counts. A meta-analysis was not done because the designs, sports, ages and programs were too heterogeneous.
paper.findings: Of the two observational studies, the larger (6,662 high school athletes) found that composite neck strength predicted concussion after adjusting for sex and sport (OR 0.95 per pound, 95% CI 0.92-0.98, p = 0.004), while a study of 130 university athletes found no link between deep neck flexor endurance and concussion. Using the reviewers' calculated risk ratios, a cluster trial of 1,355 adult rugby players showed fewer head and neck injuries (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.18-0.64) and fewer concussions (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.19-0.69), whereas in a cluster trial of 2,452 adolescent rugby players neither reduction was significant (head and neck RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.61-1.09; concussion RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.55-1.17). Two pre-post studies used historical controls: 119 high school athletes had 2 concussions against 11 expected (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.04-0.62), and 27 professional rugby players had fewer match-related cervical injuries but no significant change in total cervical injuries (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.30-1.87).
paper.limitations: The authors note few included studies, varied designs, small samples and heterogeneous sports and age groups, and adverse events and missing data were rarely reported. Each intervention outcome rests on only three studies (Tables 3 and 4), not four, and only the adult rugby trial gave a certain effect for head and neck injury. The Abstract says four intervention studies showed reductions, which overstates the non-significant adolescent trial and the uncertain professional rugby result.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest considering neck exercises within multi-component injury-reduction programs for contact-sport athletes, and they flag adolescent and female athletes as the groups most in need of further study. Because the evidence is limited, staff should treat neck training as one part of a broader program and track adherence, which the authors link to program effect.
paper.athleteDev: Neck strengthening can be included in contact-sport injury-reduction programs, with attention to adherence and dose. The review does not measure performance outcomes, so it does not show any performance benefit.
paper.rtp: This review concerns injury prevention and does not address return to sport after concussion. It should not be used to set return-to-play timelines or clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: Integrating intramuscular fat radiomics with hamstrings-to-quadriceps structure and function ratios to predict future hamstring strain injury.pdf

paper.citation: Sharma A, Smith DR, Slutsky-Ganesh AB, Diekfuss JA, Hogg JA, Foss KDB, et al. Integrating intramuscular fat radiomics with hamstrings-to-quadriceps structure and function ratios to predict future hamstring strain injury. PLOS Digit Health. 2025;4(12):e0001144.
paper.abstract: A prospective longitudinal study of 93 professional American football players, nine of whom sustained a hamstring strain injury during the season, tested whether MRI radiomic features of thigh intramuscular fat could predict future injury. The authors also tested whether adding muscle imbalance and injury history improved prediction, using a K-nearest neighbour classifier.
paper.tldr: In 93 professional football players, MRI texture features of hamstring fat combined with strength ratios and injury history predicted in-season hamstring strain injury with a cross-validated AUC of about 0.79. With only nine injuries, the authors say the models need validation in larger, independent groups.
paper.methods: A prospective cohort in which thigh IDEAL MRI, isokinetic knee strength at 180 deg/s and the Hamstring Outcome Score were collected from 112 athletes, with 93 having complete data. Radiomic features were extracted from hamstring and quadriceps fat-contrast images, reduced by correlation and minimum-redundancy selection, and classified with K-nearest neighbour models using 250 repetitions of three-fold cross-validation.
paper.findings: The best model, combining hamstring radiomics, muscle imbalance and injury profile, had an AUC of 0.79 (95% CI 0.78-0.80; sensitivity 78.4%, specificity 67.9%), above hamstring radiomics alone (AUC 0.68) and quadriceps radiomics alone (AUC 0.55). The hamstring-to-quadriceps torque ratio alone also had an AUC of 0.79, and it was lower in injured players (0.39 vs 0.49, p = 0.006). Injury profile alone gave an AUC of 0.67, while the HaOS score alone gave an AUC of 0.49.
paper.limitations: Only nine injuries occurred, there was no independent holdout test set because of the small event rate, and the sample was single-site, male and from one sport. The Results text gives hamstring radiomics alone as AUC 0.67 while Table 2 and the Abstract give 0.68 (0.6789), and the Abstract gives the injury profile model as 0.68 while Table 2 gives 0.67. Limb-identification models performed poorly on right-side injuries (specificity 20-25%).
paper.practicalImplications: Hamstring fat texture, the hamstring-to-quadriceps torque ratio and injury history are candidate risk markers worth testing in larger cohorts. The paper does not support using these models to flag individual players, since the best model misclassified 22% of injured players and 32% of uninjured players.
paper.athleteDev: Injured players had lower hamstring torque and a lower hamstring-to-quadriceps torque ratio, but the paper does not test whether training changes these measures or affects performance.
paper.rtp: The study predicts future injury and does not evaluate return to sport. The authors suggest baseline scans could later help judge injury severity and guide clinical decisions after injury, but this was not tested and should not guide clearance.

records.sourceFile: International study of video review of concussion in professional sports.pdf

paper.citation: Davis GA, Makdissi M, Bloomfield P, Clifton P, Echemendia RJ, Falvey EC, et al. International study of video review of concussion in professional sports. Br J Sports Med. 2018.
paper.abstract: This survey of medical personnel from six professional sports compared how video review is used to identify and manage possible concussion, including the video signs, definitions, reviewer roles and protocols. Lying motionless and motor incoordination were video signs common to all six sports, and impact seizure and tonic posturing were included in the criteria for all sports except the NHL. The authors conclude that video review is well established, that the diagnostic criteria and reviewer expertise are not clearly established, and that sports should work towards a common standard.
paper.tldr: Professional sports use video review for concussion in different ways, and the signs and removal rules differ between codes. Only lying motionless and motor incoordination are common to all six sports, so one sport's protocol should not be assumed to transfer to another.
paper.methods: Senior medical advisers and chief medical officers from seven major codes were invited, and all seven responded; MLB was excluded because it does not use video review, leaving six sports. Each sport completed a standardised questionnaire on video source, video signs, definitions, biomechanical criteria, reviewer qualifications, spotters, time limits, equipment, education and compliance between November and December 2017. Two researchers extracted the data independently, and a narrative synthesis compared definitions across sports.
paper.findings: All six sports use live in-game video review. Lying motionless and motor incoordination are common to all six sports, and impact seizure and tonic posturing are in the criteria for all sports except the NHL. Only three sports include a biomechanical video criterion, and most sports mandate permanent same-game removal for some video signs; the NHL does not mandate permanent removal from video alone and instead uses a standardised assessment.
paper.limitations: This is a descriptive census of protocols reported by medical personnel from six codes, with no athlete data and no data on how accurately reviewers identify video signs. The authors note that there is no validated biomarker of concussion, so video studies carry the risk of false positives and false negatives. The paper reports practice as of 2018 and does not examine whether private viewing areas change reviewer performance.
paper.practicalImplications: Medical staff should know which video signs trigger permanent removal and which trigger removal and assessment under their own governing body's protocol, because these differ between codes. Where possible, reviewers should have access to multiple camera angles and variable-speed playback, as the authors recommend. The paper supports a conservative approach to lying motionless, tonic posturing, impact seizure and motor incoordination on video, but does not show that any of these signs confirms a concussion.
paper.athleteDev: This is not a performance paper. It may help performance and sports science staff understand the game-day video review process they support, but it does not address training or performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: It can inform on-day decisions about permanent removal versus removal and assessment after a suspected concussion. It cannot be used to set return-to-play timelines or recovery criteria, because it reports protocols and does not evaluate recovery.

records.sourceFile: Intra‑ and Inter‑Muscular Variations in Hamstring Architecture and Mechanics and Their Implications for Injury- A Narrative Review.pdf

paper.citation: Kellis E. Intra- and Inter-Muscular Variations in Hamstring Architecture and Mechanics and Their Implications for Injury: A Narrative Review. Sports Med. 2018.
paper.abstract: This narrative review examines intra- and inter-muscular variation in the architecture and mechanical properties of the hamstrings. The biceps femoris long head has the shortest and most pennated fibres, the semimembranosus differs in proximal attachment and moment arm, and the semitendinosus shows less relative strain for the same joint motion. The author concludes that some architectural variations may help explain why some muscles are injured more than others, and that interventions targeting specific muscles or regions should be tested.
paper.tldr: The hamstring muscles differ in fibre length, pennation, tendon and moment arm, so one exercise is unlikely to load all of them in the same way. These differences may help explain injury patterns, but the link to injury has not been tested directly.
paper.methods: This narrative review drew on studies found by searching SPORTDiscus and MEDLINE from 1966 to October 2017 with terms for hamstring architecture, anatomy, mechanics, strain and injury. Studies were included if they related to hamstring architecture, anatomy or mechanical properties. The review summarises findings by muscle, tendon, muscle-tendon unit mechanics and fascicle-tendon interaction, with tables of architecture values reported across studies.
paper.findings: The biceps femoris long head has the shortest and most pennated fibres and is injured more often than the other hamstrings, while the semitendinosus has the longest muscle-tendon unit and fascicles and the least relative strain for the same joint motion. Values for the same parameter vary widely between studies; for example, the reported pennation angle of the biceps femoris long head ranges from 0 to 28 degrees. The semitendinosus is divided into two compartments by a tendinous inscription, but the functional role of these compartments in humans is unclear.
paper.limitations: Most of the evidence comes from cadaver, imaging and modelling studies, and the author attributes much of the variation in reported values to where and at what joint position measurements were taken. Several conclusions rest on assumptions, such as that fibre length governs excursion and pennation governs force, and the tendon and aponeurosis properties of each hamstring are not fully known. The search covered two databases only, and no quality appraisal of the included studies is described.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners should recognise that the hamstrings do not all respond the same way to one exercise, which the author suggests may justify exercises or rehabilitation aimed at specific muscles or regions. This is a hypothesis for future research and not a proven prescription, because the review does not show that targeted programmes reduce injury or speed recovery. When interpreting published architecture values or individual imaging, staff should allow for the wide variation between studies.
paper.athleteDev: The review suggests that different hamstring exercises may load each muscle differently, which could matter when designing strength work for sprinting and high-speed running. It does not test any training programme or measure performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: It can inform the question of whether rehabilitation after a hamstring injury should target the specific muscle or region involved, as the author suggests. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria, because the review contains no outcome data on rehabilitation, recovery or re-injury.

records.sourceFile: Is Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP)                        Effective in the Treatment of Acute Muscle Injuries_  A            Systematic        Review     and Meta-Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Grassi A, Napoli F, Romandini I, Samuelsson K, Zaffagnini S, Candrian C, et al. Is Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Effective in the Treatment of Acute Muscle Injuries? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2018.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials evaluated platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections for acute muscle injuries compared with placebo injection or physical therapy. Six trials with 374 patients were included. The authors found that PRP shortened time to return to sport across all trials, but that this effect was not supported when only double-blind trials or hamstring-only trials were considered, and that re-injury and complication rates were similar between groups.
paper.tldr: Across six randomized trials, PRP for acute muscle injuries shortened time to return to sport only when all trials were pooled, and the effect was not significant in blinded trials. PRP did not reduce re-injury, and the evidence was rated low to very low quality.
paper.methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA, searching PubMed, CENTRAL and Web of Science, plus grey literature and reference lists, to 1 November 2017. Randomized trials of PRP for acute muscle injuries with a placebo or physical therapy control were included. Return to sport was pooled as a mean difference and re-injury and complications as risk differences, with sensitivity analyses by blinding and injury site, risk of bias assessed with the Cochrane tool, and evidence graded with GRADE.
paper.findings: Across all six trials, PRP shortened time to return to sport (mean difference -7.17 days, 95% CI -12.26 to -2.08; I2 = 95%). This was not significant in the two double-blind trials (mean difference -5.65 days, 95% CI -12.14 to 0.84) or in the three hamstring-only trials (mean difference -5.95 days, 95% CI -12.48 to 0.57). Re-injury (risk difference -0.03, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.05) and complications (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.06) did not differ, and pain was reported as better with PRP in three of five trials, mostly in the first three weeks.
paper.limitations: The review includes only six trials with 374 enrolled patients, and the authors state the time-to-return data were not normally distributed, which may bias the parametric analysis. Reporting is inconsistent: Table 1 and the abstract show four trials without patient blinding while Section 3.6 says three, and the text's analysed group sizes (145 PRP, 191 control) do not match the Table 2 totals (163 and 170 included, 157 and 161 at follow-up). The review was not registered in PROSPERO.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors conclude that the large and indiscriminate use of PRP for acute muscle injuries is not justified and that use should be limited to controlled trials until better evidence emerges. Because adverse effects were negligible, PRP is low risk, but the faster return it suggests should not be relied on, since it was not significant in blinded trials.
paper.athleteDev: Four studies found no strength difference at final follow-up, and only one small trial reported early strength and range-of-motion gains with PRP, so PRP should not be expected to improve physical performance on return. Staff should not plan return-to-play timelines around a PRP-related gain, because the time benefit was not significant in the blinded trials.
paper.rtp: The review addresses return to sport after acute muscle injury and found a shorter time to return across all trials, but this was not significant in the double-blind trials, which the authors rate as moderate-quality evidence of no difference. It should not be used to set a faster return-to-play timeline, and it does not support PRP for reducing re-injury, which did not differ between groups.

records.sourceFile: Is it really the result of a concussion - Lessons from a case study.pdf

paper.citation: McGeown JP, Hume PA, Kara S, Neary JP, Gardner W. Is it really the result of a concussion? Lessons from a case study. Sports Medicine - Open. 2019;5:8.
paper.abstract: This case study used an interdisciplinary assessment to determine the cause of persistent symptoms in a man with multiple sports-related concussions. The Neary neurophysiological protocol and a concussion clinic assessment showed no impairment in the neurophysiological tests, and specialist assessment identified peripheral vestibular and otolithic dysfunction seemingly unrelated to his concussion history. The authors conclude that persistent symptoms that patients attribute to concussion may have unrelated causes with similar symptoms, and that multi-disciplinary assessment with repeated testing is important.
paper.tldr: In one 40-year-old man with persistent symptoms and a history of 10 self-reported sport concussions, a full multi-disciplinary work-up identified a vestibular and otolith cause that seemed unrelated to his concussion history. The authors argue persistent symptoms should not be assumed to come from concussion without a complete assessment.
paper.methods: Single-case short communication with ethics approval and written consent for publication. The participant completed the Neary protocol twice (7 and 20 March 2018), which assesses neurophysiological responses over about 60 minutes, followed by a concussion clinic assessment, neurology review with structural MRI, and a dizziness and balance centre assessment including vestibular and audiology tests.
paper.findings: The Neary protocol assessments showed no notable impairment, and he performed within normative limits on all concussion clinic tests; his concussions had all occurred before age 30, resolved within days or weeks, and his current symptoms began at 33. The MRI and neurological examination were normal apart from a minor note of fluid in the inner ear, and specialist testing found unilateral tinnitus, an asymmetric hearing profile and otolithic dysfunction that reproduced his symptoms during gait with large head movements. He was diagnosed with peripheral vestibular disturbance and started an exercise programme to load the otolith, with follow-up every three to four weeks; outcomes are not reported.
paper.limitations: This is a single case with no control group, and the authors state that the attribution of his symptoms to a non-concussion cause cannot be made with absolute certainty. The discriminatory value of the Neary protocol is not established, blood pressure monitoring was not performed, and the response to the exercise programme is not reported.
paper.practicalImplications: When an athlete with prior concussions reports persistent symptoms, staff should not assume that concussion is the cause without a multi-disciplinary assessment that checks for other causes, such as vestibular or otolith problems. Referral to a neurologist, vestibular therapist or other specialist should be considered when the symptoms do not fit a concussion pattern, and the assessment should be repeated.
paper.athleteDev: The case does not bear on performance training. For staff, the point is that symptoms an athlete attributes to past concussions may need medical assessment before any change to training load is based on them.
paper.rtp: The paper gives no return-to-play criteria and reports no outcome from the exercise programme, so it cannot inform a return-to-sport timeline. Its message for return-to-sport decisions is that persistent symptoms in an athlete with prior concussions should be assessed for other causes before they are attributed to concussion.

records.sourceFile: Is the acute-chronic workload ratio associated with risk of time loss injury in professional team sports - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Andrade R, Wik EH, Rebelo-Marques A, Blanch P, Whiteley R, Espregueira-Mendes J, et al. Is the Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR) Associated with Risk of Time-Loss Injury in Professional Team Sports? A Systematic Review of Methodology, Variables and Injury Risk in Practical Situations. Sports Medicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: This PROSPERO-registered systematic review summarised the methods used to calculate the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) and its association with time-loss injury in adult professional or elite team sport athletes. Twenty longitudinal studies with 2,375 injuries from 1,234 male athletes were included. The majority of studies found a higher injury risk at a higher ACWR relative to a lower or moderate ACWR, but the methodological approaches varied widely and limit the strength of recommendations.
paper.tldr: Across 20 studies of professional male team-sport athletes, a higher acute:chronic workload ratio was usually linked to more time-loss injuries, but the methods varied so much that no cut-off could be set. Staff should manage workload spikes and build chronic load, not apply a fixed ACWR threshold.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42017067585) searching PubMed, EMBASE and OpenGrey from inception to 31 May 2019 for longitudinal studies of ACWR and time-loss injury in adult professional or elite team sport athletes. Two reviewers screened and extracted data, and a third resolved disagreements. Study quality was rated with a modified Downs and Black checklist, and results were summarised by workload metric, without a meta-analysis.
paper.findings: Ninety percent of studies showed a positive association between a higher ACWR (relative to a low or moderate ACWR) and a higher risk of injury, and two studies found no significant association. A low ACWR was linked to higher risk in only a few studies, and when combined with low chronic load, high or low ACWR was associated with increased risk in four studies. Most studies used a coupled ACWR with weekly blocks, a 1-week acute and 4-week chronic window, and the subsequent week as the injury lag, and none used time-to-event analysis. In one example, a high total distance ACWR above 2.0 was associated with about a fivefold increased risk, corresponding to a 4% injury likelihood versus 1% at a moderate ACWR.
paper.limitations: The review could not pool results because the studies used different sports, ACWR calculations, binning methods and injury definitions, and it excluded adolescents, recreational players and non-time-loss injuries. Most included studies did not adjust for confounders, did not report power calculations, and did not describe how missing data or transferred players were handled, and all included studies used male athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: The ACWR can be used as a planning tool to flag sharp workload spikes during the season, after injury and after the off-season, but it should not be used alone to judge individual injury risk. Staff should report the ACWR method they use, including coupling, averaging method and window lengths, because the results depend on these choices. The authors do not support a single cut-off, and staff should note that a large relative increase can still mean a low absolute injury risk.
paper.athleteDev: The review supports monitoring workload spikes using the ACWR, but it does not support a single prescribed cut-off. The authors argue that developing higher chronic load helps athletes tolerate the acute loads of competition, so chronic load building should be planned alongside spike management.
paper.rtp: The authors suggest the ACWR could help plan load when athletes return to competition after injury, but no included study tested this and the review reports no return-to-play outcomes. It cannot establish safe return-to-play thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Ischiofemoral impingement and hamstring syndrome as   causes of posterior hip pain.pdf

paper.citation: Martin HD, Khoury A, Schröder R, Palmer IJ. Ischiofemoral Impingement and Hamstring Syndrome as Causes of Posterior Hip Pain: Where Do We Go Next? Clin Sports Med. 2016;35:469-486.
paper.abstract: No structured abstract is printed. The key points state that deep gluteal syndrome can be associated with ischiofemoral impingement and hamstring syndrome, that six physical examination tests help diagnose these conditions, and that non-operative and operative treatment depend on the differential diagnosis and contributing anatomy.
paper.tldr: Posterior hip pain can come from deep gluteal syndrome, ischiofemoral impingement or hamstring syndrome, and these can coexist. A structured history, a set of hip examination tests and imaging help separate them before treatment is chosen.
paper.methods: Narrative clinical review by the authors, who describe anatomy, biomechanics, history and examination, imaging, and non-operative and operative treatment. No systematic search is described. Test accuracy values are taken from cited studies.
paper.findings: The review reports the cited accuracy of several tests: long stride-walking test sensitivity 0.94 and specificity 0.85; IFI test sensitivity 0.82 and specificity 0.85; active piriformis test sensitivity 0.78 and specificity 0.80; piriformis stretch test sensitivity 0.52 and specificity 0.90. It also describes an endoscopic lesser trochanteroplasty series in which modified Harris Hip Score, VAS and return to sport improved at 2 years.
paper.limitations: No described search method and no evidence grading. The IFI validation cited uses 17 patients with IFI. The authors' own clinical observation on lesser trochanter version is noted as needing further study. The text does not report the issue number.
paper.practicalImplications: When posterior hip pain is reported, the review advises a full hip examination that includes the long stride-walking test, the IFI test and piriformis tests, with imaging to rule out intrapelvic causes. Non-operative care combines physical therapy, guided injections and a home programme for sciatic nerve mobility.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the review explains how to tell IFI, proximal hamstring syndrome and deep gluteal syndrome apart when an athlete reports sitting pain or pain lateral to the ischium. It gives no athlete performance or load data.
paper.rtp: The review gives no return-to-sport criteria. It cites one endoscopic IFI series that reported return to sport, and its post-operative tables give rehabilitation timelines (for example 12 weeks for IFI, and 24 weeks to 2 years for deep gluteal syndrome). These are clinical planning guides, not validated return-to-sport tests.

records.sourceFile: JUSTHO~1.PDF

paper.citation: Bullock GS, Mylott J, Hughes T, Nicholson KF, Riley RD, Collins GS. Just How Confident Can We Be in Predicting Sports Injuries? A Systematic Review of the Methodological Conduct and Performance of Existing Musculoskeletal Injury Prediction Models in Sport. Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of the methodological conduct and completeness of reporting of musculoskeletal injury prediction models in sport. Thirty studies (204 models) were included. Most used regression and some used machine learning. None externally validated a model, and most were rated high or unclear risk of bias. The authors conclude no model can be recommended for practice.
paper.tldr: Most published sports injury prediction models were poorly developed, have a high risk of bias and have not been externally validated. None can be recommended for practice yet.
paper.methods: Systematic review using PRISMA and CHARMS, with PROBAST risk of bias. Medline, EMBASE, CENTRAL, SPORTDiscus and CINAHL were searched from inception to 24 June 2021, with two reviewers screening and extracting data. Studies needed a sport injury prediction model using regression, machine learning or deep learning.
paper.findings: Of 30 studies, 18 used regression only, 4 machine learning only, 7 both, and 1 regression, machine learning and deep learning. No model was externally validated. Two studies (7%) were rated low risk of bias overall and 28 (93%) high or unclear. Internal validation was performed in 14 studies, calibration was reported in 3, and 2 studies cited or discussed TRIPOD. No machine learning study reported tuned hyperparameters or code. The median events per parameter was 2.7.
paper.limitations: The Methods list five databases, but the flow diagram shows three and the Discussion says only three were included. The Discussion names studies 42 and 39 as low risk while Results and Table 3 list 37 and 39, the count of studies using both regression and machine learning is given as seven and as eight, calibration is reported in two studies (abstract) or three (Results), and the Key Points say 79% of studies were high risk versus 93% high or unclear in the Results. The review was limited to English-language, peer-reviewed articles.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use the reviewed injury prediction models to make load or training decisions for athletes. If a model is considered, check its development, reporting and external validation first, using the review's criteria, and be cautious where sample sizes are small.
paper.athleteDev: The review gives no model to use for injury-risk decisions in performance programmes. Screening outputs from small, unvalidated models should not drive training load changes without checking how they were built.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return-to-sport decisions. The reviewed models predict new injury rather than readiness after injury, and the review finds none suitable for practice.

records.sourceFile: Lack of proprioceptive strategy modulation leads to at risk biomechanics for anterior cruciate ligament in healthy athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Picot B, Lempereur M, Morel B, Forestier N, Rémy-Néris O. Lack of Proprioceptive Strategy Modulation Leads to At-Risk Biomechanics for Anterior Cruciate Ligament in Healthy Athletes. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2024;56(5):942-952.
paper.abstract: Forty-seven handball players performed anticipated and unanticipated side-cutting, and were classified as flexible or rigid by their proprioceptive postural strategy on firm and foam surfaces. Pelvic and lower-limb kinematics, kinetics and EMG of seven muscles were compared between profiles and between cutting conditions using statistical parametric mapping.
paper.tldr: Handball players who could not shift their balance control away from the ankle (rigid profile) showed muscle activity and ankle rotation patterns linked to ACL injury risk during side-cutting. These are laboratory markers, not injury outcomes.
paper.methods: Forty players (aged 15 to 25, with at least two years of high-level experience) were grouped as flexible or rigid from their postural response to muscle vibration on firm and foam surfaces. They then performed three anticipated and five unanticipated side-cutting trials, interspersed with straight runs. Kinematics and kinetics were recorded with a 3D motion system and force plates, and EMG was recorded from seven muscles, with two-way statistical parametric mapping for group and condition effects.
paper.findings: Rigid players showed less semitendinosus (P<0.001) and less vastus lateralis (P<0.05) preactivity 200 to 100 ms before initial contact, more gluteus medius preactivity, and more ankle internal rotation before contact. About 70 ms after contact they showed higher vastus lateralis activity (P<0.001) and more ankle internal rotation (-8.49 vs -3.17 degrees at 75 ms). Knee moments and kinematics did not differ between profiles, and unanticipated cuts showed less ipsilateral pelvic tilt before contact and more vastus lateralis activity about 50 ms after contact, with no interaction between profile and condition.
paper.limitations: Laboratory tasks may not reproduce match conditions. EMG was normalized to the anticipated-cut peak and interpreted as activation, not force, and only the dominant limb was analysed. Seven players were removed by the 95 to 105 percent cut-off, and no injury outcomes were measured. The abstract reports higher vastus lateralis activity in rigid players (P=0.032), while the results text reports lower vastus lateralis preactivity before contact and higher activity after it; the results values are used here.
