paper.practicalImplications: Screening for proprioceptive strategy with vibration and foam-surface testing could identify players whose cutting patterns may need attention. The authors propose a targeted neuromuscular program for rigid players and cues to keep the ankle in neutral rotation during stance. These are proposals and were not tested in this study.
paper.athleteDev: Cutting drills for handball and other field sports could target ankle rotation and hamstring preactivation in side-cutting, which the authors identify as the key differences in rigid players. The study did not test whether training changes these patterns, so treat the drills as a hypothesis to monitor.
paper.rtp: No injured or post-operative players were studied and no return-to-sport outcomes were measured. The study cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria or to judge readiness after ACL reconstruction.

records.sourceFile: Late swing or early stance A narrative review of hamstring injury mechanisms during high‐speed running.pdf

paper.citation: Kenneally-Dabrowski CJB, Brown NAT, Lai AKM, Perriman D, Spratford W, Serpell BG. Late swing or early stance? A narrative review of hamstring injury mechanisms during high-speed running. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2019;29:1083-1091.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of biceps femoris long head musculotendon mechanics and muscle excitation during high-speed running, and how they may relate to injury timing. It contrasts a late-swing mechanism (large eccentric force, peak strain and negative work) with an early-stance mechanism (high hamstring loads from ground reaction forces), and concludes that late swing is the most likely injury phase while noting that direct evidence is lacking.
paper.tldr: Most of the evidence points to late swing, when the hamstring lengthens under large force and strain, as the likely injury phase in high-speed running. Direct evidence is still lacking, and early stance remains a plausible alternative.
paper.methods: Searches of Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed using combinations of hamstring, injury, sprint, run, EMG, activity, kinematic and kinetic terms, plus manual checks of reference lists. The review synthesises hip and knee kinematics and kinetics, EMG excitation, musculoskeletal-model estimates of musculotendon length and force, and the few prospective and case-based injury studies. No pooled analysis is reported.
paper.findings: Model estimates show the biceps femoris long head reaches peak length and strain at about 112 percent of upright muscle length in terminal swing, and musculotendon force peaks at 10.5 to 26.4 N/kg in late swing, with a smaller early-stance peak of 3 to 11.6 N/kg. Excitation in late swing is reported as two to three times that in early swing and late stance. The one prospective study (Schuermans et al, soccer players) found kinematic differences in later-injured players only during the swing phase.
paper.limitations: Musculotendon findings depend on model assumptions and on filtering choices that may under-estimate early-stance force. The injury-timing conclusions rest partly on speculative mechanisms and on a few injury cases, and the authors state that direct evidence is lacking. The paper is labelled a narrative review, and the search terms and databases are reported without a formal appraisal of study quality.
paper.practicalImplications: A late-swing focus supports prioritizing exercises that lengthen the hamstring fascicles, a principle the authors cite from other literature. The review does not test any specific exercise or program, and the authors call for prospective musculoskeletal-model studies before the timing question can be settled.
paper.athleteDev: Use the late-swing framework when reviewing sprint mechanics, paying attention to hip flexion, then knee and hip extension, in terminal swing. The review gives no validated screen, so any such assessment remains a coaching judgement.
paper.rtp: The review addresses injury mechanism only. It does not evaluate return to sport, reinjury or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot be used to decide when an athlete is ready to sprint after a hamstring strain.
